The provided text contains front matter, including library stamps and title pages [PDF p. 2-3, 11]. The author, C. W. C. Oman, provides a preface arguing that the Byzantine Empire should no longer be viewed as merely decadent or monotonous [PDF p. 13]. He contends that recent scholarship has demonstrated the empire's vital role in resisting the Saracens and preserving learning [PDF p. 13]. The author acknowledges his reliance on various chroniclers, such as Procopius and Anna Comnena, to justify his narrative [PDF p. 14]. A detailed table of contents follows, outlining the history from the foundation of Byzantium through the fall of Constantinople in 1453 [PDF p. 15-20]. Additionally, a list of illustrations describes various coins, maps, and artworks used within the volume [PDF p. 21-24].

The narrative begins with the founding of Byzantium by Greek colonists from Megara approximately 2,558 years ago [PDF p. 27]. These settlers established a colony on a headland near the Golden Horn [PDF p. 27]. According to legend, the Delphic oracle instructed them to build their city opposite the "city of the blind," referring to Chalcedon [PDF p. 29]. The author notes that Byzantium's location offered significant military and commercial advantages [PDF p. 30]. It commanded Black Sea trade and served as a vital frontier fortress [PDF p. 30-31]. Throughout its early history, the city maintained independence except for brief periods of Persian rule [PDF p. 31]. The text describes how the city survived various sieges and conflicts involving Athens and Macedonia [PDF p. 32-34]. After falling to Alexander the Great, Byzantium eventually became a free confederate city under Rome [PDF p. 34]. However, Emperor Vespasian later stripped the city of these privileges [PDF p. 34].

The city faced significant destruction in A.D. 196 when Emperor Severus punished its resistance [PDF p. 35]. Although it recovered, Byzantium remained a target for Goths and usurping emperors [PDF p. 36]. The text details how Licinius used the city as a chief fortress before Constantine the Great besieged and captured it in A.D. 323 [PDF p. 37-38]. Oman interprets Constantine as a practical, unsympathetic leader who sought a more convenient administrative center than Rome [PDF p. 39-41]. Constantine chose Byzantium because of its superior military and commercial positioning [PDF p. 42-43]. He established the new capital with great energy, marking its boundaries through solemn processions [PDF p. 44].

The topography of the new Constantinople included a central marketplace marked by the Milion [PDF p. 44-45]. The imperial palace occupied a vast precinct near the shore [PDF p. 45]. Public life centered on the Augustaeum, which contained the Baths of Zeuxippus and the Senate House [PDF p. 45-47]. The author notes that the Bishop's palace was overshadowed by the imperial residence, limiting spiritual independence [PDF p. 47-48]. A major feature was the Hippodrome, where chariot racing fueled intense factional rivalries between the Blues and Greens [PDF p. 48-49]. These factions often caused public disorder and political instability [PDF p. 49-50]. The Hippodrome's central division wall featured an Egyptian obelisk and a three-headed brazen serpent [PDF p. 50].

The supplied material ends mid-description of the monuments within the Hippodrome. Consequently, the full history of the empire and the complete topographical details remain unresolved in this excerpt.

The Hippodrome contained several ancient monuments, including a golden tripod dedicated at Delphi in 479 B.C. [PDF p. 51]. While the vast walls had crumbled, central decorations like the square bronze column remained [PDF p. 51]. Along the eastern wall stood various statues and the Milion, the empire's central milestone [PDF p. 51]. Constantine added a porphyry column featuring an image originally representing the Apollo of Hierapolis [PDF p. 51]. North of the Hippodrome sat the original, humbler Hagia Sophia, which was later destroyed by fire [PDF p. 52]. A wooden gallery connected this church to the Royal Gate of the palace [PDF p. 52].

Constantine chose Byzantium as his capital around A.D. 328 or 329 [PDF p. 54]. He held a consecration festival on May 11, 330, featuring Christian services [PDF p. 54]. To populate the city, Constantine offered privileges to senators, merchants, and artisans [PDF p. 55]. He also transferred the Egyptian wheat-tribute to Constantinople to ensure food supplies [PDF p. 55]. Although an edict named the city New Rome, people primarily called it Constantinople [PDF p. 56]. After Constantine died in A.D. 337, civil wars eventually left Constantius II as sole ruler [PDF p. 57].

The empire faced threats from the east and north [PDF p. 58]. While Sapor of Persia challenged the eastern frontier, the Goths posed a northern danger [PDF p. 58]. By A.D. 376, the Huns had driven the Visigoths toward the Roman Danube border [PDF p. 61]. The Emperor Valens allowed the Goths to enter as subject-allies [PDF p. 62]. However, corruption by officials like Lupicinus led to starvation and revolt [PDF p. 63]. This culminated in the disastrous Battle of Adrianople in A.D. 378, where Valens was killed [PDF p. 65, 67]. Theodosius later stabilized the region by enlisting Gothic war-bands into the Roman army [PDF p. 68].

The author argues that this policy of using barbarian auxiliaries under their own chiefs was dangerous [PDF p. 70]. Following Theodosius' death in A.D. 395, factional wars erupted between German and Roman parties [PDF p. 73]. Alaric led the Visigoths in revolt, eventually invading Italy [PDF p. 74, 75]. Meanwhile, Gainas attempted to seize power in Constantinople but was defeated by a local mob [PDF p. 76, 77]. The empire stabilized under the reorganization of Leo I, Zeno, and Anastasius [PDF p. 85]. These rulers utilized native troops, such as Isaurians, to reduce barbarian influence [PDF p. 87].

Justinian ascended the throne in A.D. 527 after his uncle Justinus died [PDF p. 91]. He married Theodora, a former actress, which caused significant social scandal [PDF p. 92, 93]. The author describes Justinian as a hard, suspicious, and tireless ruler [PDF p. 95]. His foreign policy aimed to reunite the Western Mediterranean provinces with the East [PDF p. 99]. Early in his reign, he fought an indecisive war against the Persian King Kobad [PDF p. 100]. This conflict highlighted the military merit of his general, Belisarius [PDF p. 100].

The text does not provide information regarding the ultimate outcome of Justinian's wars or his later reign.

The provided text details the political and military transitions of the Byzantine Empire during the sixth century [PDF p. 101]. The narrative begins with the Nika riots in A.D. 532, which were fueled by the Blue and Green circus factions [PDF p. 101]. These groups had evolved from sporting factions into political parties with religious affiliations [PDF p. 101]. Following a botched execution of rioters, the city experienced six days of violent unrest [PDF p. 102]. The rebels demanded the removal of unpopular officials and attempted to install Hypatius as Caesar [PDF p. 102]. During this chaos, fires destroyed much of the city, including the cathedral of St. Sophia [PDF p. 103]. While ministers urged Justinian to flee, Empress Theodora famously refused to abandon her position [PDF p. 105]. This resolve prompted a final assault led by Belisarius, who routed the rebels in the Hippodrome and killed approximately 35,000 people [PDF p. 105-106].

The author then transitions to Justinian's foreign conquests, noting that the suppression of internal dissent allowed for imperial expansion [PDF p. 107]. Belisarius first conquered the Vandal kingdom in Africa by A.D. 534, taking King Gelimer captive [PDF p. 111-112]. The text argues that the Vandals were particularly vulnerable due to their small numbers and fanatical religious views [PDF p. 110]. Subsequently, Belisarius invaded Italy to challenge the Ostrogoths [PDF p. 114]. Although he captured Rome and Ravenna, the conquest was not permanent [PDF p. 115, 117]. The author interprets the Gothic failure as a result of religious and racial tensions between Arians and Orthodox Catholics [PDF p. 109]. Furthermore, the rise of the noble Baduila temporarily restored Gothic control before he was eventually defeated by Narses in A.D. 553 [PDF p. 118-121]. The Italian campaign left the region depopulated and devastated [PDF p. 122].

The final sections examine the decline of Justinian's reign, which was marred by a devastating plague starting in A.D. 542 [PDF p. 127]. This pestilence caused massive mortality and weakened the empire's organizational capacity [PDF p. 127-128]. Simultaneously, Chosroes of Persia launched an invasion that sacked Antioch [PDF p. 125]. Although Belisarius eventually secured a peace treaty in A.D. 545, the empire remained financially and militarily strained [PDF p. 126]. Following Justinian's death, the empire faced new threats from the Lombards in Italy and the Avars and Slavs in the Balkans [PDF p. 141]. The author describes the Slavs as a rude, unorganized people who used unconventional tactics like hiding in water to ambush Romans [PDF p. 149]. The text concludes by noting that while the Balkan provinces were inhabited by Latin-speaking provincials, these new migrations threatened the Roman character of the region [PDF p. 150].

The source contains some historical uncertainties, such as the specific methods used by the Slavs to conceal themselves in water [PDF p. 149]. It also notes that certain legends regarding Belisarius's poverty may be untrue [PDF p. 131].

The Latin-speaking population of Thrace and Illyria faced severe devastation during the Slav and Avar invasions between 570 and 600 [PDF p. 151]. The author notes that these newcomers were more savage than previous Gothic invaders [PDF p. 151]. Contemporary chronicler John of Ephesus describes how the Slavs overran Thrace and Greece, capturing cities and settling by force [PDF p. 151]. While fortified towns resisted, the open country was swept bare [PDF p. 152]. General Priscus attempted to hold the Danube, but Roman population limits eventually fell back to the Balkans [PDF p. 152].

The failure to stem these invasions contributed to the fall of Emperor Maurice [PDF p. 152]. Although Maurice was a capable officer and author of the *Strategicon*, he lost the respect of his soldiers [PDF p. 153]. In 602, his order for the Danube army to winter north of the river led to a revolt [PDF p. 153]. The troops elected Phocas as their leader and marched on Constantinople [PDF p. 153]. After Maurice fled to the Asiatic provinces, Phocas captured and executed him and his five sons [PDF p. 153]. The author characterizes Phocas as a brutal and reckless usurper whose reign caused the empire to fall apart [PDF p. 154]. Phocas's rule was marked by executions, including those of Maurice's widow and the general Narses [PDF p. 154]. This instability prompted Chosroes of Persia to declare war under the pretext of avenging Maurice [PDF p. 155]. Persian forces eventually reached the gates of Chalcedon in 608 [PDF p. 155].

In 610, Heraclius took the throne after his father, the exarch Heraclius, sent a fleet to overthrow Phocas [PDF p. 156]. Heraclius inherited an empire in chaos, with provinces overrun by Persians, Avars, and Slavs [PDF p. 157]. The loss of Jerusalem in 614 and the seizure of the "True Cross" by Shahrbarz caused widespread despair [PDF p. 158]. This crisis sparked a surge of national and religious feeling [PDF p. 159]. Heraclius led several campaigns, eventually defeating the Persians through skillful strategy and attacking their heartland in Media [PDF p. 161]. By 628, Chosroes was overthrown by his son Siroes, and a peace treaty restored Roman territory and the "True Cross" [PDF p. 164].

The empire's recovery was short-lived as the Saracen invasion began [PDF p. 166]. Heraclius faced these new enemies while the empire was financially drained and religiously divided [PDF p. 187]. The Arabs captured Syria and Egypt, including Jerusalem in 637 [PDF p. 189]. Following Heraclius's death in 641, his successors struggled with internal court intrigues caused by the marriage of Heraclius to his niece, Martina [PDF p. 190]. Constantine IV later achieved great fame by defending Constantinople against a massive Arab siege using "Greek-fire" [PDF p. 196]. The empire also faced new threats from the Bulgarians in the late seventh century [PDF p. 197]. Finally, Justinian II ascended the throne as a reckless tyrant who depleted the treasury through extortion and unsuccessful wars [PDF p. 199].

The text does not provide information regarding the ultimate fate of Justinian II or the long-term resolution of his conflicts.

The provided text details a period of intense political instability and religious conflict within the East-Roman Empire. Following unsuccessful wars against the Saracens, Justinian II began executing or imprisoning his officers [PDF p. 201]. In 695, an officer named Leontius seized power after receiving counsel from a monk named Paul [PDF p. 201]. Leontius deposed Justinian II, mutilated his nose, and banished him to Cherson [PDF p. 201]. This usurpation initiated twenty years of anarchy characterized by constant revolts and foreign defeats [PDF p. 202]. During this time, Saracen armies ravaged the Asiatic frontier and captured Carthage in 697 [PDF p. 202].

The instability continued when the admiral Tiberius Apsimarus seized Constantinople and proclaimed himself Tiberius III [PDF p. 203]. Although Tiberius III achieved some military successes against the Saracens, he remained a precarious ruler [PDF p. 203]. Meanwhile, the exiled Justinian II escaped from Cherson by killing two Khazar officers sent to seize him [PDF p. 204]. He eventually secured Bulgarian support and returned to Constantinople in 705 to reclaim his throne [PDF p. 205]. His restoration triggered a reign of terror where he executed former usurpers and many prominent citizens [PDF p. 205]. This era ended in 711 when Philippicus seized power and beheaded Justinian II [PDF p. 206].

The subsequent years were marked by further chaos under ephemeral rulers like Anastasius and Theodosius III [PDF p. 207]. Amidst this decay, Leo the Isaurian rose to power in 717 after defeating Theodosius III [PDF p. 208]. Leo faced a massive Saracen invasion led by Moslemah and Suleiman, but he successfully defended Constantinople [PDF p. 211]. The author argues that Leo's victory delivered Christendom from the Moslem danger [PDF p. 213]. Beyond military defense, Leo initiated the Iconoclastic movement to combat image-worship and perceived superstitions [PDF p. 215]. This policy caused significant social unrest and opposition from the monks and the Papacy [PDF p. 219].

The Isaurian dynasty concluded with a violent family tragedy involving Empress Irene and her son, Constantine VI [PDF p. 224]. Following this, the Macedonian dynasty began with Basil the Macedonian, who established a long-lasting line [PDF p. 240]. The text notes that the empire experienced a literary revival under later rulers like Leo VI and Constantine VII [PDF p. 241]. These "literary emperors" produced significant works on warfare, administration, and court ceremonies [PDF p. 243, 246]. By the ninth century, art also improved as the classical tradition revived in manuscript illumination [PDF p. 249].

The source provides detailed accounts of political successions and religious struggles but lacks specific details regarding Leo's administrative reforms [PDF p. 220]. The author notes that monkish chroniclers often obscured Leo's good deeds to emphasize his religious persecutions [PDF p. 220].

The Byzantine Empire maintained strength through a commercial monopoly centered on the Bosphorus [PDF p. 251]. This trade dominance allowed the empire to endure harsh taxation systems [PDF p. 251]. During the reign of Constantine Porphyrogenitus, the Caliphate fractured into several weak, competing states [PDF p. 252]. This fragmentation provided an opportunity for Byzantine expansion [PDF p. 253]. The general Nicephorus Phocas exploited this situation by conquering Crete in 961 A.D. [PDF p. 254]. He later led successful campaigns in Cilicia and Northern Syria [PDF p. 255]. Following the unexpected death of Romanus II, Phocas became emperor alongside the young Basil II and Constantine VIII [PDF p. 255]. Phocas was a dedicated soldier but faced domestic unpopularity due to his stern administration [PDF p. 256]. He was eventually murdered in 969 by his wife Theophano and John Zimisces [PDF p. 258, 259].

John Zimisces proved to be an effective ruler despite his violent accession [PDF p. 259]. His most notable achievement was defeating the Russian invasion led by King Swiatoslaf in 971 [PDF p. 260, 261]. This victory eventually led to the Christianization of the Russians and their integration into Byzantine culture [PDF p. 263]. Zimisces died after a short illness, leaving Basil II as his ward [PDF p. 265]. Basil II, known as the "Slayer of the Bulgarians," conducted a thirty-four year war against King Samuel [PDF p. 266, 267]. Basil eventually conquered Bulgaria and established the border at the Danube [PDF p. 268]. He also expanded into Armenia, though the author questions if this was beneficial [PDF p. 269].

The Macedonian dynasty ended with the death of Theodora in 1057 [PDF p. 274]. This extinction triggered a period of civil war and foreign invasion [PDF p. 275]. The Seljouk Turks began devastating Asia Minor, culminating in the decisive Byzantine defeat at Manzikert in 1071 [PDF p. 277, 278, 280]. Romanus Diogenes was captured during this battle and later blinded by John Ducas [PDF p. 280, 281]. Alexius Comnenus eventually stabilized the empire through a mixture of diplomacy and treachery [PDF p. 283]. He managed both the Seljouk threat and Norman invasions from Italy [PDF p. 284, 285]. While the Crusades helped push back the Turks, they also caused a terminal decline in Constantinople's commercial wealth [PDF p. 293, 294].

The Comneni dynasty saw varying levels of success under John II and Manuel I [PDF p. 295, 296]. Manuel was a brave cavalry officer but a reckless statesman whose defeat at Myriokephalon weakened the realm [PDF p. 297, 298]. After his death, the usurper Andronicus Comnenus ruled through terror before being killed by a mob [PDF p. 299]. The empire then passed to the incompetent Isaac and Alexius Angelus [PDF p. 300]. The author argues that the empire's condition was not hopeless during their reign [PDF p. 300]. However, these triflers failed to defend the state against impending destruction [PDF p. 300].

The provided text does not address the eventual outcome of the Latin conquest or the specific fate of the Angelus brothers beyond their incompetence.

The reigns of Isaac and Alexius Angelus were characterized by personal indulgence and imperial decline [PDF p. 301]. The empire suffered from military and financial disorganization following the loss of Asian recruiting grounds to Seljouk invasions [PDF p. 301]. This forced a reliance on foreign mercenaries who often became disorderly or mutinous [PDF p. 301]. Administratively, Isaac Angelus auctioned public offices and allowed officials to extort provincials [PDF p. 302]. Alexius Angelus similarly relied on rapacious favorites who dispensed patronage for bribes [PDF p. 302].

Isaac's reign saw the loss of Bulgaria and Cyprus [PDF p. 303]. A Bulgarian rebellion grew because Isaac appointed incompetent generals [PDF p. 303]. Meanwhile, Isaac Comnenus established an independent "Empire of Cyprus," a phenomenon the author describes as monstrous and abnormal [PDF p. 303]. This revolt was ended when Richard Coeur-de-Lion seized the island after the rebel maltreated English crews [PDF p. 304]. In 1195, Alexius Angelus deposed and blinded his brother Isaac through a palace intrigue [PDF p. 304].

The Fourth Crusade arrived in 1203, driven by Venetian interests and the promises of the young Byzantine exile, Alexius Angelus [PDF p. 305]. The Crusaders, led by Henry Dandolo, Boniface of Montferrat, and Baldwin of Flanders, signed a treaty to restore the Angeli in exchange for massive subsidies [PDF p. 307]. During the first siege, Venetian forces used light towers to storm the sea-walls, causing a great fire [PDF p. 310]. The cowardly Alexius III fled, leading the garrison to restore Isaac II [PDF p. 310]. However, the Crusaders felt cheated of a full sack and spent months extorting wealth from the restored rulers [PDF p. 311]. This financial pressure caused a revolt in January 1204, during which Alexius Ducas murdered both Isaac and his son [PDF p. 311].

The Latin Empire was established under Baldwin of Flanders but remained perpetually unstable [PDF p. 318]. The empire struggled against Bulgarian incursions and the loss of territory to various Greek successors [PDF p. 321]. Theodore Lascaris founded the successful Empire of Nicaea in 1206, checking Frankish expansion in Asia [PDF p. 324]. Meanwhile, Michael Angelus established a despotate in Epirus [PDF p. 326]. The Nicaean ruler John III Ducas eventually asserted dominance over the Epirot claimants [PDF p. 327].

The empire was finally reconquered by Michael Paleologus in 1261 after he usurped the throne from the child John IV [PDF p. 330]. However, the restored empire faced permanent commercial and territorial decay [PDF p. 334]. The author argues that the loss of maritime trade monopolies to Italian republics made administrative reform impossible [PDF p. 336]. Michael Paleologus further weakened the state by disarming the Bithynian militia, which facilitated Ottoman expansion [PDF p. 339]. Under Andronicus II and III, the Seljouk Turks and later the Ottomans systematically seized Byzantine lands in Asia Minor [PDF p. 341, 345]. The rise of Orkhan saw the establishment of the disciplined Janissary corps through a system of tribute-children [PDF p. 350].

The provided text does not address the eventual fall of the Ottoman Empire or the long-term fate of the remaining Greek enclaves.

The provided text details the decline of the Byzantine Empire through the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries [PDF p. 351]. Following the death of Andronicus III in 1341, the empire faced instability due to a minority reign under John III [PDF p. 351]. The author identifies John Cantacuzenus as a primary cause of destruction [PDF p. 351]. Although a clever courtier, Cantacuzenus lacked the abilities of a statesman or general [PDF p. 351]. He attempted to imitate Michael VIII by seeking to supplant his young master [PDF p. 351]. After failing to seize the capital, he summoned Servian King Stephen Dushan and Turkish princes for aid [PDF p. 352, 353]. The author argues that these alliances preserved Cantacuzenus but destroyed the empire [PDF p. 353]. While Dushan expanded his realm, his death in 1355 led to a rapid Servian collapse [PDF p. 354]. Meanwhile, Turkish incursions under Orkhan and Amour devastated Thrace and facilitated the slave trade [PDF p. 353, 354]. A hollow peace was reached in 1347, leaving the empire reduced to Constantinople, Adrianople, Thessalonica, and the Peloponnesus [PDF p. 354].

The conflict continued when John Paleologus sought to dethrone his guardian in 1354 [PDF p. 355]. Cantacuzenus utilized Orkhan's troops, but a surprise attack allowed Paleologus to seize Constantinople and capture the usurper [PDF p. 355]. Following his removal, Ottoman forces established a permanent foothold at Gallipoli under Suleiman [PDF p. 355]. Under Murad I, the empire became a mere head without a body as Thrace fell to the Turks [PDF p. 356]. The author notes that John V remained a vassal of the Turk [PDF p. 356]. This period included the humiliation of Philadelphia, where the Emperor was forced to assist in subduing a Christian stronghold [PDF p. 356].

The narrative concludes with the fall of Constantinople on May 29, 1453 [PDF p. 373]. Constantine XI faced an assault by seventy thousand troops led by Mohammed II [PDF p. 372]. Despite efforts by defenders like Giustiniani, Turkish artillery breached the walls [PDF p. 372, 373]. The Emperor died in the breach during a final Janissary assault [PDF p. 374]. Following the victory, Mohammed II entered St. Sophia and proclaimed the Islamic faith [PDF p. 375]. The text includes a table of emperors [PDF p. 377] and an index [PDF p. 379].
